latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Translocation or direct inoculation of Candida from gastrointestinal mucosa, skin, catheter biofilm, abdominal leak, urinary tract, or another focus into the bloodstream. This is the gateway mechanism for candidemia.
Active viable yeast burden in blood and vascular compartments; drives culture positivity, systemic inflammatory response, and probability of hematogenous metastatic seeding.

Adherence and biofilm growth on central venous catheters, hemodialysis catheters, implanted ports, prosthetic valves, or cardiac devices. Biofilm protects Candida from host clearance and antifungals, sustaining candidemia until source control is achieved.

Dectin-1, complement, macrophage, monocyte, and neutrophil activation by Candida cell-wall beta-glucan and mannan. Produces fever, tachycardia, leukocyte response, CRP rise, and sepsis physiology, often with lower procalcitonin than bacterial sepsis.
Distributive shock, microvascular dysfunction, capillary leak, AKI, ARDS, encephalopathy, and coagulopathy driven by invasive Candida bloodstream infection and host inflammatory response.

Ongoing candidemia despite systemic antifungal exposure because of retained infected catheter, undrained abdominal focus, infected thrombus, endocarditis, resistant isolate, or delayed active therapy.

Bloodstream spread to eye, heart valves, venous thrombi, liver, spleen, kidney, bone, joint, CNS, or implanted material. Risk rises with persistent candidemia, neutropenia, heavy burden, and delayed active antifungal therapy.
Hematogenous seeding of choroid, retina, and vitreous producing chorioretinitis, endophthalmitis, macular involvement, and vision loss risk. Ocular penetration varies strongly by antifungal class.

Candida adherence to valves, prosthetic material, pacemaker leads, vascular grafts, or infected venous thrombi, producing persistent candidemia, embolic phenomena, and high mortality without device removal or surgery when indicated.

Species- and isolate-level resistance or reduced susceptibility that weakens antifungal killing: azole resistance in C. glabrata, C. krusei, C. auris, some C. parapsilosis; echinocandin resistance after exposure or in C. auris; amphotericin susceptibility variability.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Candida entry into blood is the direct upstream event for viable bloodstream burden.
Biofilm on catheter or prosthetic material continuously sheds yeast into blood.
Retained infected material or undrained focus sustains candidemia despite systemic drug exposure.
Resistance or reduced susceptibility lowers the probability that the chosen antifungal regimen is microbiologically active.
Inactive or weak antifungal exposure converts initial candidemia into persistent candidemia and increases metastatic risk.
Fungal cell-wall beta-glucan and mannan trigger innate inflammatory signaling.
Sustained invasive candidiasis can produce septic shock and organ dysfunction, especially in critically ill hosts.
Blood culture growth is the defining microbiologic evidence for candidemia, although sensitivity is imperfect and may be reduced by prior antifungal exposure.
Circulating fungal cell-wall beta-D-glucan often rises in invasive candidiasis, but false positives occur with some exposures and it is not species-specific.
Persistently positive daily or every-other-day blood cultures measure failure of clearance and prompt search for uncontrolled source.
Persistent catheter or deep focus requires source control in candidemia.
Candidemia can arise from an obstructed, catheterized, or diabetic urinary tract; pyuria, dysuria, urinary retention, or urinary instrumentation raise this source probability.
Longer candidemia duration increases the probability of metastatic seeding to eye, heart, liver, spleen, bone, joint, and thrombus.
Choroidal circulation is vulnerable to hematogenous Candida seeding.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: amplified by prosthetic valve, intracardiac device, hemodialysis catheter, injection drug use, or persistent candidemia
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bloodstream Candida can adhere to damaged endocardium or prosthetic material and form bulky vegetations.
Persistent candidemia seeds sterile organs and implants, producing deep-seated invasive candidiasis.
Ocular seeding manifests as Candida chorioretinitis with or without vitritis.
Chorioretinal lesions are the usual ocular manifestation before vitreous extension.
Vitreous extension marks more severe endophthalmitis and reduces adequacy of echinocandin-only ocular treatment.
Ocular seeding produces an event risk that changes treatment penetration requirements and duration.
Valve or lead seeding produces Candida endocarditis, especially when candidemia persists.
Candida endocarditis often forms large vegetations because yeast and fibrin-platelet biofilm persist on valves and prosthetic material.
Endovascular seeding creates a high-mortality complication requiring prolonged therapy and possible surgery.
Catheter-associated infected venous thrombus is a classic cause of persistent candidemia.
Infected thrombus sustains candidemia and can embolize or require vein excision/drainage.
Line-associated Candida biofilm is represented by catheter infection probability and differential culture context.
Candida biofilm on central venous catheters is a common source of candidemia.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: fever may be blunted in profound neutropenia, steroids, elderly patients, or renal failure
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Innate cytokines reset the hypothalamic set point and cause febrile episodes.
Fever, cytokines, and sepsis physiology drive tachycardia.
Systemic inflammation and metabolic stress increase respiratory drive.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: baseline neutropenia or marrow suppression can make WBC low despite invasive infection
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Emergency myeloid response raises WBC when marrow reserve is present.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: profound neutropenia is a host-state modifier rather than evidence against candidemia
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Candida clearance depends heavily on neutrophils; non-neutropenic hosts often show neutrophilia.
IL-6 acute-phase signaling raises CRP in invasive candidiasis but is nonspecific.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: typically lower than bacterial sepsis at comparable severity, but may rise with shock or bacterial co-infection
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Procalcitonin can rise in candidemia, especially critical illness, but weakly separates fungal from bacterial sepsis.
Distributive shock lowers MAP through vasodilation and capillary leak.
Shock physiology lowers systolic pressure when compensation fails.
Tissue hypoperfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction elevate lactate in Candida septic shock.
Sepsis-associated AKI and nephrotoxic exposures raise creatinine.
Shock and AKI reduce urine output.
Sepsis-associated consumption, marrow stress, and critical illness thrombocytopenia lower platelets.
Candida septic shock, nephrotoxic antifungals, and critical illness increase AKI event risk.
Sepsis capillary leak and critical illness raise ARDS risk.
Severe candidemia can contribute to sepsis coagulopathy and DIC physiology.
Candidemia in critically ill hosts can progress to vasopressor-requiring shock.
Short-term mortality is dominated by septic shock, organ failure, delayed active therapy, and uncontrolled source.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: most typical during neutrophil recovery after prolonged neutropenia
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Hepatic and splenic microabscesses can emerge after bloodstream Candida in neutropenic or hematologic malignancy contexts.
Candida endocarditis and infected thrombus carry high mortality and recurrent embolic/source-control risk.
Severe systemic infection, shock, hypoxemia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, or fluid overload can increase oxygen or ventilatory support needs; this parallels the existing ards_hazard pathway.
Innate cytokine response to candidemia drives fever.
Candida biofilm on central venous catheters is a common source of candidemia.

axes.shape_free_text: Fever is common but may be absent or blunted in neutropenia, steroids, elderly patients, renal failure, or critical illness.
Sinus tachycardia during fever, shock, or critical illness; may be medication-blunted.
Tachypnea tracks sepsis physiology, metabolic acidosis, or ARDS.

Oxygen or ventilatory support requirement: 0 room air, 1 low-flow nasal cannula, 2 mask or higher low-flow support, 3 high-flow nasal cannula, 4 noninvasive ventilation, 5 invasive ventilation or extracorporeal support.
Falls in Candida septic shock; may require vasopressor support when fluid-unresponsive.
Low systolic pressure reflects distributive shock or mixed critical illness physiology.
Elevates with shock, hypoperfusion, and mitochondrial stress; persistent elevation indicates high mortality risk and inadequate resuscitation/source control.
Can be high, normal, or low depending on marrow reserve; neutropenia is a major host-state modifier rather than evidence against candidemia.
Non-neutropenic hosts may show neutrophilia; profound neutropenia strongly changes prior, presentation, dissemination risk, and duration of therapy.
Nonspecific acute-phase response; often elevated but does not distinguish candidemia from bacterial sepsis.
Usually lower than bacterial septic shock at similar clinical severity, but may rise in severe candidemia, renal failure, mixed infection, or critical illness.
Thrombocytopenia from sepsis, critical illness, DIC physiology, marrow disease, chemotherapy, or flucytosine toxicity.
Rises with sepsis-associated AKI, baseline CKD, amphotericin nephrotoxicity, or hemodynamic instability.
May fall with severe candidemia-associated sepsis physiology, dehydration, renal failure, hyperglycemia-related translocational hyponatremia, or critical illness.
Rises when candidemia presents with severe AKI, shock, acidosis, urinary obstruction, or renal replacement need; baseline may be strongly modified by CKD or diabetes.
Stress hyperglycemia and uncontrolled diabetes are common contexts for invasive Candida, especially urinary or ICU presentations.
Oliguria tracks shock and AKI.
May rise with cholestasis, hepatic dysfunction, TPN, biliary source, septic shock, or azole hepatotoxicity.
Mild-moderate transaminitis from sepsis, hepatobiliary source, azoles, echinocandins, or amphotericin formulations.
Low albumin reflects critical illness, inflammation, malnutrition, liver disease, capillary leak, or chronic comorbidity and increases free drug/toxicity context.
Probability that blood cultures grow Candida; one positive sterile blood culture is clinically meaningful, but sensitivity is imperfect.
Supportive fungal biomarker; elevated in many invasive fungal infections and has false positives from dialysis filters, some blood products, gauze, and certain antibiotics.
Number of days after active therapy start with ongoing Candida-positive blood cultures; persistence after about day 3-5 suggests source failure, resistance, or deep focus.
Probability that the current systemic antifungal regimen has in-vitro and tissue-site activity against the Candida isolate.
Probability that the Candida isolate is susceptible or susceptible-dose-dependent enough for fluconazole exposure to be clinically active.
Probability that micafungin, anidulafungin, caspofungin, or rezafungin is active against the isolate.
Probability that lipid amphotericin B has microbiologic activity against the isolate.
Probability that the isolate is Candida auris or clinically managed as C. auris pending confirmation; drives isolation, public health reporting, and resistance expectations.
axes.ontology_note: Candida species identity is post-workup microbiology/pathogen identity; treatment implications are handled separately by treatment modifiers.

axes.shape_free_text: Probability that the isolate is Candida glabrata; increases azole resistance concern and may require higher-dose or non-azole therapy.
axes.ontology_note: Candida species identity is post-workup microbiology/pathogen identity; treatment implications are handled separately by treatment modifiers.

axes.shape_free_text: Probability that the isolate is Candida parapsilosis; strongly associated with catheter biofilm and can have higher echinocandin MICs or emerging azole resistance.
axes.ontology_note: Candida species identity is post-workup microbiology/pathogen identity; treatment implications are handled separately by treatment modifiers.

axes.shape_free_text: Probability that the isolate is Candida krusei; implies intrinsic fluconazole resistance.
axes.ontology_note: Candida species identity is post-workup microbiology/pathogen identity; treatment implications are handled separately by treatment modifiers.

axes.shape_free_text: Presence of central venous catheter, hemodialysis catheter, port, PICC, or similar intravascular line during candidemia.
Probability that an intravascular catheter is the primary source or sustaining reservoir.
Probability that the line is infected, supported by catheter-tip culture, differential time to positivity, exit-site infection, or candidemia persistence with retained line.
Need for removal, drainage, debridement, device extraction, thrombus management, or other non-drug source intervention.
Adequacy of catheter removal, abdominal drainage/debridement, device extraction, and control of infected thrombus or deep focus.
Probability that candidemia is driven by abdominal surgery, anastomotic leak, peritonitis, necrotizing pancreatitis, abscess, or undrained abdominal collection.

Probability that candidemia is driven by candiduria with urinary obstruction, retention, catheterization, diabetic urinary dysfunction, or urologic instrumentation rather than catheter or abdominal source.
Drainable intra-abdominal collection or abscess that can sustain invasive candidiasis.
Mucositis, neutropenic enterocolitis, GI surgery, bowel ischemia, perforation, pancreatitis, or leak creating Candida translocation risk.
Current or recent TPN exposure through central access, increasing Candida growth and catheter-associated candidemia risk.
Recent broad-spectrum antibacterial exposure selecting for Candida colonization and overgrowth.
ANC under roughly 0.5 x 10^9/L or anticipated prolonged neutropenia, modifying prior, fever threshold, dissemination, and duration until recovery.
Any sterile-organ or implanted-material Candida focus beyond uncomplicated bloodstream infection.
Ophthalmologist-confirmed Candida chorioretinitis or endophthalmitis after candidemia.
Chorioretinal Candida lesion without requiring vitreous extension; a specific ocular dissemination pattern.
Vitreous involvement from Candida endophthalmitis, changing local therapy and vitrectomy need.
Candida native valve, prosthetic valve, or device-associated endocarditis by echo, operative, or microbiologic evidence.
Largest Candida vegetation size on echocardiography; larger vegetations increase embolic and surgical-source-control pressure.
Infected venous thrombus associated with candidemia, often catheter-associated and a cause of persistence.
Event rate of AKI during candidemia, shock, nephrotoxic therapy, or amphotericin exposure.
Event rate of ARDS from severe sepsis, capillary leak, transfusion, volume overload, or mixed infection.
Event rate of overt sepsis-associated DIC during severe candidemia or mixed infection.
Event rate of progression to vasopressor-requiring septic shock.
Event rate of developing Candida ocular involvement after candidemia.
Event rate of clinically meaningful vision loss from macular chorioretinitis or vitritis.
Event rate of Candida endocarditis or intracardiac device infection.
Event rate of Candida-infected venous thrombus, especially with retained catheter or persistent candidemia.
Event rate of chronic disseminated hepatosplenic candidiasis, especially during neutrophil recovery after prolonged neutropenia.
Bleeding event rate from catheter removal, drainage, surgery, vitrectomy, dialysis catheter placement, or anticoagulation context.
Baseline or acquired QTc risk that increases azole arrhythmia toxicity and monitoring needs.
Severe hepatic dysfunction that changes azole and echinocandin toxicity, monitoring, and dose choices.
Severe kidney dysfunction or dialysis that changes fluconazole/flucytosine dosing and amphotericin toxicity.
Pregnancy or near-term pregnancy planning changes azole and amphotericin risk-benefit context.

Lifespan outcome hazard for candidemia; driven by shock, organ failure, persistent candidemia, delayed active antifungal therapy, inadequate source control, resistant species, and deep metastatic foci.
Oral thrush is a structured host-context clue for advanced cellular immunodeficiency or Candida overgrowth; it is not a disease-specific mechanism for this leaf.
Candida bloodstream infection commonly produces fever despite antibacterial therapy.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and tachycardia co-vary after accounting for shared cytokine drive.
Hypotension and lactate elevation co-move in septic hypoperfusion.
Oliguria commonly precedes measurable creatinine rise in sepsis-associated AKI.
Longer candidemia duration increases metastatic seeding probability.
Persistent blood cultures trigger search for removable line, infected thrombus, endocarditis, or undrained focus.
Adequate catheter removal or focus drainage shortens candidemia duration.
Ocular Candida involvement can progress to vision loss, especially with macular or vitreous disease.
Vitritis increases organism burden behind the blood-ocular barrier and raises visual complication risk.
Candida endocarditis raises mortality through persistent fungemia, embolization, valve destruction, and surgery need.
Infected thrombus can shed Candida for days to weeks without mechanical source control.
Shock is a dominant near-term mortality driver in candidemia.
AKI marks severe organ dysfunction and can limit antifungal options.
Coagulopathy increases bleeding risk from catheter procedures, drainage, vitrectomy, and surgery.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Echinocandin activity is broad and fungicidal for most Candida bloodstream isolates.
C. parapsilosis often has higher echinocandin MICs and strong catheter biofilm association.
Echinocandins have limited ocular penetration; ocular involvement requires eye-penetrating systemic and sometimes intravitreal therapy.

failure_modes: retained infected catheter or prosthetic material
ocular, CNS, or endocardial focus requiring additional penetration or source control
C. parapsilosis with high MIC and persistent candidemia
treatments.context_specific_role: Broad early systemic Candida killing while species and susceptibility data are pending.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rezafungin shares echinocandin target biology with once-weekly exposure.
Ocular disease needs agents with ocular penetration or local therapy.

side_effects.interpretation: Hepatic enzyme monitoring as with other echinocandins

treatments.context_specific_role: Long-interval echinocandin option when weekly pharmacokinetics are operationally useful.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluconazole only clears candidemia reliably when the isolate is susceptible and adequate exposure is achieved.
Persistent candidemia argues against step-down until clearance and source control are documented.
Azoles can prolong QTc and interact with other QT-prolonging drugs.
Fluconazole is renally cleared and requires dose adjustment.

failure_modes: azole-resistant C. glabrata or C. auris
ongoing shock or persistent blood cultures
QTc or major CYP drug interaction

side_effects.interpretation: QTc prolongation and CYP-mediated interaction risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral or IV azole path when isolate susceptibility, clinical stability, clearance, and source control support it.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Voriconazole can be useful for susceptible C. krusei and has better ocular penetration than echinocandins.
Triazoles have hepatic metabolism, hepatotoxicity, and major interaction burden.

failure_modes: subtherapeutic or toxic levels without monitoring
treatments.context_specific_role: Selected azole path for susceptible non-fluconazole scenarios and ocular-penetration needs.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Liposomal amphotericin B retains broad Candida activity and is used when azole/echinocandin pathways are limited.
Amphotericin exposure can worsen kidney injury even in lipid formulation.
Amphotericin-based treatment is important for resistant ocular disease and can be paired with local therapy.

failure_modes: electrolyte wasting not captured by current axes
treatments.context_specific_role: Broad systemic alternative when resistance, intolerance, pregnancy context, CNS/ocular/endovascular disease, or treatment failure makes azole or echinocandin paths inadequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Flucytosine is mainly an adjunct in selected deep, CNS, ocular, or endovascular Candida infection rather than routine uncomplicated candidemia.
Renal impairment markedly increases flucytosine accumulation and marrow toxicity risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Synergy add-on for selected resistant or deep Candida foci with therapeutic drug monitoring and renal adjustment.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Source control is causal when the line, abdominal collection, infected thrombus, device, or focus sustains candidemia.
Candida catheter biofilm cannot be sterilized reliably by systemic antifungals alone.
Undrained abdominal collections require drainage or debridement for definitive control.

failure_modes: unsafe removal because of limited access

side_effects.interpretation: Bleeding from catheter removal, drainage, or debridement

treatments.context_specific_role: Remove or drain the sustaining focus: catheter removal/exchange, abscess drainage, debridement, device extraction planning, or thrombus/source procedure as indicated.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vitritis or macular threat requires local drug levels and sometimes vitrectomy.
Local therapy targets vision-threatening ocular burden.

side_effects.interpretation: Intravitreal injection or vitrectomy procedural bleeding/retinal complication risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Local ocular intervention when Candida endophthalmitis threatens macula or involves vitreous.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Valve or device infection often cannot be cured with drugs alone, especially prosthetic material or large vegetations.
Severe coagulopathy or prohibitive operative risk can delay or preclude surgery.

side_effects.interpretation: Cardiac or vascular procedure bleeding risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical cure path for Candida endocarditis, infected cardiac devices, infected vascular grafts, or refractory infected thrombus.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluid resuscitation targets sepsis-induced hypoperfusion.

side_effects.interpretation: Over-resuscitation can worsen pulmonary edema/ARDS risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Sepsis physiology support while antifungal therapy and source control reshape the disease landscape.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vasopressor support is useful only when hypotension or shock physiology is present.

failure_modes: arrhythmia or ischemia at high dose

side_effects.interpretation: Excess vasoconstriction can worsen ischemic injury when doses are high

treatments.context_specific_role: Hemodynamic bridge for Candida septic shock while the causal antifungal/source-control path takes effect.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: KRT supports severe AKI complications but does not treat Candida burden.

side_effects.interpretation: New dialysis catheter can become an additional intravascular source if prolonged

treatments.context_specific_role: Organ support for severe AKI, refractory acidosis, electrolyte derangements, or volume overload during candidemia.

supportive_care: Obtain at least two blood culture sets before antifungal therapy when this does not delay unstable-patient treatment; repeat blood cultures daily or every other day until clearance is documented.

Request Candida species identification and susceptibility testing for bloodstream isolates, including azole susceptibility and echinocandin susceptibility when prior echinocandin exposure, C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. auris, persistence, or local resistance patterns make it relevant.

Search for a removable or drainable source: review all vascular catheters, ports, hemodialysis access, TPN lines, abdominal drains, surgical sites, anastomotic leaks, urinary obstruction, and implanted devices.
Remove or exchange central venous catheter as early as safely feasible when it is a likely source or candidemia persists.
Evaluate persistent positive blood cultures after about day 3-5 for infected catheter, septic thrombophlebitis, endocarditis, abdominal abscess, urinary obstruction, or antifungal resistance.
Perform ophthalmology evaluation for ocular dissemination; in neutropenia, ocular findings can be delayed until neutrophil recovery.
Use echocardiography when candidemia persists, prosthetic valve or cardiac device is present, embolic signs occur, new murmur or heart failure appears, or no source is found.
Image abdomen/pelvis or other symptom-directed sites when there is abdominal surgery/leak, persistent fever, focal pain, neutropenia recovery fever, or persistent candidemia.
Track MAP, lactate, urine output, creatinine, platelets, bilirubin, ALT, and oxygenation to detect shock, AKI, DIC physiology, hepatic toxicity, and ARDS.
Renal-dose adjust fluconazole and flucytosine; monitor amphotericin nephrotoxicity and echinocandin/azole hepatic toxicity.
Monitor QTc and drug interactions when azoles are used, especially with transplant immunosuppression, antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, macrolides, or fluoroquinolones.
Do not treat Candida isolated only from respiratory secretions as candidemia evidence; treat sterile-site and bloodstream evidence in clinical context.

For uncomplicated candidemia without deep focus, duration is anchored to bloodstream clearance and symptom resolution; deep ocular, endovascular, bone, joint, CNS, or hepatosplenic involvement requires longer focus-specific treatment.

Use sepsis organ-support bundle when shock is present: balanced crystalloid, vasopressor support to adequate perfusion, lactate reassessment, oxygen/ventilation support, renal support if indicated, and glycemic control.

Apply Candida auris infection-control measures when C. auris is suspected or confirmed: contact precautions, environmental cleaning with active disinfectants, screening of contacts per local public health guidance, and reporting as required.

Consult infectious diseases for candidemia management, antifungal selection, source-control coordination, duration, and resistance handling; involve ophthalmology, surgery, interventional radiology, cardiology, or cardiac surgery according to focus.
